prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant quantum spin Hall insulator and its Z2 classification, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B004 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a single prize part. The round-1 exchange has, if anything, sharpened the case. Four of us now prefer it with identical laureates, every member who prefers something else still lists it as a first or second alternative, and nobody has argued against its scientific standing. I do not rest on that count. The reason is the physics: Kane and Mele showed that time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling alone give a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states without a magnetic field. That was a definite prediction that could have failed, Molenkamp's group tested it in HgTe quantum wells, and about two decades of transport and ARPES work in many materials have confirmed and extended it. Following the clues in nature is what I want from a theory-led prize, and here the clue was found. The chair asks whether the citation can be defended without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. I think it can, if it is written as Johansson and Eriksson suggest: anchored on the Kane-Mele prediction and the first observation, and not on the design of the HgTe heterostructure. The citation above is worded that way and is deliberately limited to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, so that three-dimensional topological insulator work is not drawn in.
statement.case_against: I keep the two reservations and want them recorded openly, not argued away. First, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp tested; Zhang is deceased, and a three-name limit forces the committee to draw a boundary that excludes a decisive contributor to the experimental realisation. I consider this a real weakness of the allocation, and I am not claiming that the narrow citation removes it, only that it keeps the citation truthful about what is credited. Second, the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and phases of matter makes B004 look to some like a return to the same theme. I read the Z2 classification as a distinct step because it concerns symmetry-protected boundary states without quantised Hall conductance from a field, but a colleague who weights continuity of prize lineage heavily is not being unreasonable. Neither point is disqualifying in my judgement. If the committee decided that the credit gap was disqualifying, I would move to B006 on attribution grounds, not to B009.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the 2005 and 2012 citations do not cover the lattice architecture or the 10^-18 regime, and that the redshift and constant-variation physics now being done with lattice clocks is new, so the adjacency to earlier prizes is not decisive.
responses.response: That answers most of the objection I raised in round 1. I accept that Katori's magic-wavelength idea is an architecture and not a refinement of the comb or of ion control, and that the pair is the cleanest allocation on the shortlist. What it does not yet answer is the chair's question about what the citation would say that does not reach back into the comb or the ion-clock lineage; a citation anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice would be defensible. I still weigh the conceptual step in B004 more heavily than precision, even spectacular precision, because B004 changed what condensed-matter physicists search for. But the difference is smaller than I wrote in round 1, and B006 is now my first alternative because its attribution is cleaner than that of B004.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B009, arguing that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 discovery is a clean theory-plus-experiment match, that the pairing mechanism is a question about a derived phase and not about the discovery, and that waiting for a mechanism may mean waiting indefinitely.
responses.response: I take the last point seriously and I agree that the mechanism need not be settled for a prize on flat-band correlated physics. My concern is different and is not about superconductivity. The decisive experiments are seven or eight years old, the intrinsic phenomenology is entangled with twist-angle disorder and strain, and the experimental credit would rest on Jarillo-Herrero alone, without Cao and the MIT co-authors, which you also acknowledge. That makes B009 harder to defend today than B004, where the interpretation has been tested for nearly two decades. I have moved B009 up to second alternative, which reflects that your argument has force. I do not move it above B004, and I note that you accept B004 is the safer choice on maturity.

responses.point: Johansson keeps B004 first but wants the citation drawn tightly around the Z2 quantum spin Hall prediction and its first observation so that three-dimensional work is not drawn in, and rejects B043 because source identification still rests on few associations.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow wording and have adopted it in the citation, which now refers only to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall insulator and its first observation. I also accept your reading of my own B043 position: the diffuse flux is firmly established, but TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are few associations at moderate significance, and I should not ask the committee to prize leadership of a very large collaboration while DUMAND and Baikal founders are left out. I have therefore dropped B043 from my alternatives this round. I do not regard the BHZ gap as disqualifying, but I would not say, as I think you come close to saying, that a narrow citation solves it. It only makes the boundary explicit.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from B002 to B004 because the sharp, falsifiable prediction and its experimental confirmation make it a prize for a discovery and not a research programme, and asks that the credit boundary be stated openly in the record; he also keeps B043 only as an alternative because of his own affinity.
responses.response: I agree that it should be stated openly, and I would support recording in the committee's own text, not only in the citation, that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route, that Zhang is deceased, and that the credited trio was chosen for the Z2 prediction and its first observation. On B043 I accept your caution and share it. I would add that your disclosed astroparticle background is a reason for the committee to read your opinion on B043 with that in mind, not a reason to discount it, and neither of us now treats it as a ready first choice.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B006 and names continuity with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main objection the committee must answer, while stating that the line between lattice clocks and the single-ion lineage is a judgement call and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
responses.response: Your framing is the honest one, and it is the reason I treat B006 as a serious alternative and not as a lesser one. Where we differ is on how much the unrealised redefinition of the second should count. I do not think prospective impact is a point against a discovery prize, and a clean two-name allocation is a genuine advantage over B004. My difference with you is limited to the weight of the conceptual step: I read B004 as opening a larger programme of symmetry-protected matter, while the lattice clock is a decisive instrument achievement in an existing programme. I would not oppose B006 if the committee judges that attribution cleanliness should decide, and your Tokyo and JSPS disclosure does not seem to me to call for recusal on its own.

uncertainties: How much weight the 2016 topological-matter prize should carry against the Z2 classification as a distinct conceptual step; this is a judgement and not a fact I can establish from the supplied material.

Whether a narrow two-dimensional citation can honestly separate the credited trio from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or whether the committee will regard the omission as disqualifying, in which case I would favour B006.
Whether the lattice clock is a new concept or a precision step within the 2005 and 2012 lineage; I have moved toward the first reading but have not fully settled it.
I cannot independently verify the priority claims around the 3D generalisation and the first ARPES observations from the supplied text.
Whether B043 will mature enough in a later year through firmer source identification and KM3NeT cross-checks.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B004, B006 or B009. My documented connections are to David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is a credited candidate on this shortlist. I have no recorded connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Katori or Ye. My string theory and cosmology background is not directly relevant to any shortlisted part, and I have no private knowledge of other deliberations.
